seriesStmt.title: Acquisition
Encyclopédie des nouveaux usages des collections dans les musées d’art
Acquisition
Encyclopedia of New Uses of Collections

body.p: What new uses are emerging for the display of acquisitions? When and in what contexts are acquisitions exhibited? How do museums present or identify their new acquisitions within the galleries devoted to the collections? Can the arrival of a new work impact the presentation and experience of collections? What is the significance of novelty today or, more broadly, what is the role of displaying acquisitions in relation to the hanging of collections? Can it transform the narrative of an exhibition, opening up subjects or themes that challenge the origin and history of Western museum collections? Can exhibitions influence acquisitions, and vice versa? Can acquiring be decisive for the future direction of collections? These questions suggest that the display of acquisitions is far more complex than it may initially appear. Seldom studied within art history and museology, it is one of the forgotten aspects of the history of exhibitions and general knowledge about collections. With little documentation from museums, it often leaves few traces in the archives, even though it is an essential activity for understanding the dynamics of a collection, its history and its current relevance.

Exhibition is not necessarily the immediate fate of acquisitions. Only a tiny fraction of the collections are on display Mairesse, 2022, compared with the ever-growing number of works or objects accumulating in storage. While certain contemporary works from the 1960s onwards need to be exhibited as soon as they arrive at the museum due to their specific nature and the care required for their musealisation, these are exceptions or atypical cases. Living, variable or performative works have indeed forced museums to adapt their standards regarding acquisition, conservation and exhibition. Beyond the intrinsic nature of the works themselves, other transformations are also being felt in museums, whose effects more broadly concern the display of acquisitions.

To grasp its implications and emerging uses, it is helpful to distinguish the display of acquisitions from major redeployment projects, which unfold over long periods and occur far less frequently—for instance, during the refurbishment of a gallery devoted to the permanent collection, the construction of a new wing, a large-scale donation, or a desire to signal a shift in collection management. On the contrary, the display of acquisitions tends to be selective and strategic. It imposes a faster rhythm on the presentation of collections, in sync with the arrival of works at the museum. Historically focused on novelty, the commemorative and celebratory function associated with it is now shifting, opening collections to changes of a temporal, narrative, and discursive nature. This entry seeks to clarify how the display of acquisitions operates. Intended as a new use, it manifests itself at times radically, at times subtly. It is one of the key drivers behind the development of collections, enabling them to adapt to immediate realities, but also to be conceived, constructed and reconstructed.

div.head: Acquiring to Exhibit
div.p: Generally speaking, acquisitions are displayed in two main ways: 1) rotation or inclusion of new acquisitions in a permanent exhibition, and 2) presentation of temporary exhibitions dedicated exclusively to them. While these formats share the common aim of creating a sense of novelty and marking a moment of significance within the collections, they increasingly seek to address the social and ethical imperatives that museums now face. The generic title new acquisition, used by museums since at least the first half of the twentieth century to introduce one or several works, is still widely employed, yet it no longer appears to refer to the internal logic of the collection nor to the modern principles of avant-garde practice and enrichment. The collection is no longer merely enriched by the arrival of an acquisition; it is now transformed by it. Its display activates this transformation within the exhibition spaces.

The first approach consists in adding or replacing one or more works in the spaces devoted to the permanent collections to highlight the arrival of a new acquisition. Without altering or disrupting the existing installation, museums draw on various strategies to identify rotations and to emphasise the novelty or distinctiveness of an acquisition. Current curatorial approaches, however, tend to move away from the celebratory or glorifying function traditionally associated with novelty, instead assigning the acquisition a function of recontextualization. At the Montréal Museum of Fine Arts, this is the case for contemporary Indigenous works, which are placed in dialogue with historical Québécois and Canadian art. For instance, the large canvas The King’s Beavers (2011) by Cree-descended artist Kent Monkman was given a singular presentation at the entrance to the Founding Identities
gallery as soon as it was acquired in 2011. As the exhibition text explains, the representation of First Nations is now enhanced by the acquisition of works by contemporary artists who offer us their critical and retrospective perspective. Acquisitions thus help remedy the historical invisibility of Indigenous peoples while offering a critical rereading of a collection rooted in colonial foundations. The move from acquisition to display is particularly swift in this case: it meets a specific need and signals to audiences the significant work of revising the Museum’s collections currently under way.

The emphasis placed on the novelty of an acquisition has not disappeared; rather, it has diversified and now permeates other elements of the exhibition or interpretative apparatus, including the wall label. Discreet but widely used in all types of exhibitions, the main purpose of this small caption is to accompany an exhibited work and provide information about its identity, materiality, origin or provenance, and date of arrival in the collections: name of the artist, title of the work, date of creation, materials, dimensions, method and date of acquisition, and inventory number. This tool is increasingly being used in permanent galleries to signal the arrival of a new work, either by adding expressions such as new, recent or in the process of being acquired, or by using a distinctive visual sign that is easily recognisable. The museum thus seeks to show the movement of the works, to highlight the variation in a display without breaking or disrupting the temporal and narrative sequence.

The second approach consists in producing temporary exhibitions based exclusively on acquisitions, whether by creating spaces adjacent to the permanent collection galleries or by presenting a selection. The conception of temporary exhibitions built around acquisitions has expanded exponentially in the history of collection-based exhibitions. It contributes to increasing the percentage of works displayed, drawing attention to the arrival of works in the museum, demonstrating the dynamism of a collection, and highlighting its ever-changing nature. Breaking with the model of the permanent display, this type of exhibition signals—beginning with its very title—the unprecedented and renewable nature of the acquisition within the collection by adopting various labels of novelty. These labels are often accompanied by a subtitle indicating the department responsible for the acquisition, the artistic movement, technique or medium, and the geographical or national designation. They may also be used to emphasise the name of a major artist, the name of a donor, the funds that enabled the acquisition, the number of works displayed, or the dates of the acquisition period. Some exhibition titles also highlight the presence of key works in order to stress their novelty and exclusivity, or the singular or exceptional nature of one or more acquisitions. Thus, the display of acquisitions in the context of temporary exhibitions has mainly developed as a mirror of the collection’s ongoing flow.

This model, however, seems to be losing ground in favour of a new use of acquisitions within thematic groupings that convey alternative narratives about the collection and the museum’s heritage mission . Indeed, museums appear to be moving away from novelty while also distancing themselves from historical displays that underpin the grand narrative of art history and the museum’s authority, in order to rethink collections from a contemporary perspective and to prioritise multiple points of view. Thematic approaches, arising from curatorial choices, are increasingly common and often take the form of exhibition programmes. This is notably the case, since 2016, at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, which, through a series of temporary exhibitions entitled Here and Now at Museum Ludwig, examines works acquired through curatorial explorations conducted in collaboration with artists, curators, and researchers. Acquisitions become objects through which questions about the collection can be raised and contextualised within broader debates. The series has addressed, among other topics, the construction of modernism, the representation and exoticisation of the Global South, the questioning of the use of the category Russian avant-garde for certain works in the collection, and, for its tenth edition (in 2024), the occupation of space.

While historically the purpose of acquisition was to fill gaps in collections, some museums now acquire works primarily to mount exhibitions. Acquisitions become the driving force behind exhibition programming and a factor shaping the future direction of museum activities. The correlation between acquisition and exhibition can be taken to its extreme, as illustrated by the National Gallery of Canada, which in 2010, 2012, 2014, and 2017 presented its contemporary art acquisitions in the form of a biennale. The 2014 edition, entitled Shine a Light, brought together Canadian and Indigenous works, while in 2017, international works were added. This biennial approach to acquisitions signals contemporaneity rather than novelty and echoes the global rise of biennials as a means of presenting contemporary art from a global, and sometimes post-global and critical, curatorial perspective Weiss, R., 2011; O’Neill, Shreikh, Streeds, Wilson (ed.), 2019. The idea of organising a major event dedicated to acquisitions also emphasizes the substantial volume of works, the Museum’s social role, and the labour and expertise of curatorial teams—particularly exemplified by the 2012 edition, evocatively titled Builders.

Are curatorial practices transforming the role of acquisitions, or even changing the dynamic between exhibition and collection? Has the so-called curatorial turn, characterised by critical and reflexive approaches O’Neill, 2012, reached collections? Does it compel the museum to justify its choices and demonstrate transparency? Does it offer the display of acquisitions new contexts and possibilities for the exhibition and interpretation of collections?

div.head: Acquiring to Reinterpret
div.p: Acquisition acts as a marker of time both in the life of an artwork and in the history of the museum. While its display highlights the internal dynamics of the museum as well as the formation and development of its collections, it now also offers the institution an opportunity to showcase itself and reveal what goes on behind the scene. How is a collection formed, and who are the actors involved in its development? What are the acquisition processes, and what purposes do acquisitions serve? The museum can thus choose to present its current acquisitions, or even explain its acquisition procedures, and use an exhibition as an opportunity to look back on its past, the origins, creation and history of its collections.

In the context of a reorganisation of its permanent collections in 2015, the Musée National d’Art Moderne at the Centre Pompidou returned to a chronological arrangement of works by movement, style, and artist. A series of dossier exhibitions then interrupts the historical continuity through thematic incursions, and one instance, in 2018–2019, entitled Histoire(s) d’une collection (History/Stories of a Collection), presents a “retrospective” of the collections interspersed among the modern art masterworks galleries Les Cahiers, 2018. The Museum simultaneously exposes itself to scrutiny through its acquisition choices over time.

Several temporary projects dedicated to the history of collections have been designed from an acquisition-focused perspective: the two exhibitions Silence and Revision at the Karl Ernst Osthaus Museum in Essen in 1988 , as well as the L’Inventaire cycle at the FRAC Normandie-Rouen from 2011 to 2019. These atypical examples present collections according to the dates of acquisition. Removed one by one from storage, the works are displayed not according to historical chronology (by movement and style), but according to their acquisition date, as indicated by their inventory number Dulguerova in Fraser and Jim, 2018. In this way, the moment of acquisition becomes the guiding principle for the entire collection’s display.

More recently, curatorial approaches have sought to push the reflexivity of acquisition even further by proposing transformations of the narrative structure of collection exhibitions, interrogating the museum’s social and historical stance. The principles of novelty and enrichment take on a different significance, as museums acquire works with the aim of questioning their past, their own history, or even the Western orientation of their collections . The display of acquisitions is now framed as an ethical exercise, encouraging museums to adopt more transparent practices.

With the intention of revitalising displays of historical or ethnographic collections, some museums have taken the initiative to acquire contemporary works to be exhibited alongside older pieces. This type of juxtaposition, which suggests anachronistic and geocultural tensions, aims to refresh the presentation of historical or ethnographic collections and to legitimize their presence within institutions marked by a colonial legacy. This is the case with the Department of Historical Islamic Art at the Los Angeles County Museum, which has been acquiring contemporary works from the Maghreb and the Middle East since 2006, and the British Museum, which selects contemporary works on paper by artists from these regions based on formal characteristics shared with the objects in its material culture collection. The Montréal Museum of Fine Arts presents a similar initiative with Les arts du Tout-Monde (translated as Arts of One World), a concept introduced by the Martinican poet and philosopher Édouard Glissant. More than fifty contemporary works were specially acquired to be displayed in dialogue with ethnographic collections . By placing material culture objects and contemporary art on an equal footing, this reorganisation seeks to revisit the history of the Museum’s ethnographic collection and offer a different, updated reading. By combining historical collections with contemporary acquisitions, these anachronistic displays reveal both affinities and tensions between historical and contemporary values, tradition and modernity, Western and non-Western perspectives. Many museums that employ such anachronistic strategies were not originally intended to acquire, and even less to exhibit, contemporary art. Acquiring with the aim of rethinking the display of certain aspects of encyclopaedic collections and their universalist foundation positions the museum as an active participant in current political debates concerning the presence of ethnographic objects in Western collections.

This dialectic between acquisition and exhibition occurs in a context of not only renewal but also revision of collections. Whereas acquisitions long served to fill gaps in the chronological and canonical representation of art history—constructed around a succession of movements and the celebration of a few masterpieces—they now take on a radically different significance. Enriching the collection can signal a desire to give it a new meaning . Revisions of acquisition and collection management policies increasingly aim to achieve equity, diversity, and inclusion. While the desire to reorient acquisitions responds to both internal and external political pressures faced by museums, it simultaneously triggers changes in narrative paradigms and encourages thematic displays. In this way, an almost natural relationship seems to emerge between acquisition and exhibition. Critical stances are increasingly present within museums, particularly among curatorial teams, who seek to highlight the inadequacy of collections for revisiting history: that is, on the one hand, to take a critical look at the past, and on the other, to tell alternative stories Esner and Konijn, 2017. The aim is less to conceal the gaps in a collection than to display them as part of the construction and history of the collection itself. The case of elles@centrepompidou in 2009 is exemplary in this regard. To mount the first exhibition devoted exclusively to women artists, the Musée National d’Art Moderne had to undertake massive acquisitions in the five years preceding the exhibition’s opening. According to various sources, the new acquisitions accounted for between 30% and 40% of the works on display Dufrêne, 2014; Ernoult and Gonnard, 2009; Reilly, 2018 . The curatorial team did not seek to hide this historical bias inherent in one of the most important modern and contemporary art collections. On the contrary, remarks such as recently acquired or acquisition in progress on a large number of labels highlighted the extensive catch-up work and indicated throughout the exhibition how its curatorial design had guided acquisitions. The label does not merely indicate when a work arrived at the museum; here, it serves as a marker of new approaches to acquisitions that directly influence the direction of the collections.

This shift in perspective is particularly surprising in the treatment of large-scale acquisitions, where the sheer number of works is no longer necessarily seen as a burden, but rather as a driver of transformation. Mass acquisitions have been central to the development of museums throughout Western history and continue to be a common way of enhancing collections. Museums are often made up of collections of collections Pomian, 2009.

While the number of objects that constitutes a large-scale acquisition is not defined and there is no model to follow in this area Cheff, 1995, the inclusion of a large number of items, sometimes several hundred, very often indicates an emergency situation. Institutions must manage their intake within tight timeframes, spatial constraints in storage, and requirements for display and visibility. Mostly taking the form of pre-existing collections, sometimes even of entire museums that cannot be divided, large-scale acquisitions remain closely tied to their donating entity Lacroix, 1995. The inscription of the gift goes far beyond a mere mention on the object labels. The new corpus is usually showcased in major exhibitions dedicated to the acquisition or donation, as with the Lavalin Collection at the Musée d’art Contemporain de Montréal in 1992 and the Brigitte and Henning Freybe Collection at the Vancouver Art Gallery in 2025. By contrast, the Guggenheim UBS MAP Global Art Initiative (MAP), launched in 2012, challenged some common features of large-scale donations, notably through a process of consultation and evaluation of contemporary art acquisitions for integration into the Guggenheim Museum’s collection over a longer timeframe. Moreover, the acquisition and development process inherent to MAP did not, of course, call into question the overt relationship between the Museum and its funder, as reflected in the programme’s full title and its link to a Swiss bank.

Organised jointly by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York and UBS — a major global wealth management firm known for its involvement in major art fairs, including Art Basel — this initiative spanned six years until 2018. It offered a broad programme of activities, including three exhibitions based on acquisitions, with the aim at shedding light on three geographic regions underrepresented in Western museums: 1) South and Southeast Asia, 2) Latin America, and 3) the Middle East and North Africa . Drawing on nearly 40 million US dollars, the Guggenheim UBS MAP Purchase Fund enabled the acquisition of 126 contemporary artworks for the New York museum, helping to address certain gaps in its non-Western collection.

Before launching MAP, a consultation group was established, bringing together intellectuals and specialists from around the world to guide its collection development. This initiative activated a vast global network attuned to postcolonial and decolonial concerns, combining their perspectives and expertise with those of the Guggenheim team to generate a recent, globalised, visionary, more ethical, and exportable art collection.

Beyond enrichment aimed at diversifying the Guggenheim Museum’s collection to make it more international, MAP also involved complex geo-aesthetic considerations Barriendos, 2009, notably those arising from the circulation of exhibitions. In total, MAP generated eight exhibitions presented across six major cities: Hong Kong, London, Mexico City, Milan, New York, and Singapore. As vehicles of Western soft power, these exhibitions of new acquisitions contributed to validating artists representative of the targeted regions and to introducing them beyond their national and regional boundaries. The main areas of activity covered by MAP were assessed by the Guggenheim Museum.

Acquisition is no longer perceived merely as an addition to an existing ensemble to enhance its coherence but as a resource to diversify the collection and reposition the museum. This discussion of the display of acquisitions, from the perspective of new uses, challenges the traditional view of permanent collections as a fixed and immutable model. Instead, it highlights the flow of the collection generated by acquisitions, from arrival to display and, eventually, circulation.
